from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines_text = [
            "A distribution shows how data spreads.",
            "Uniform distributions have flat spreads.",
            "Skewed distributions are lopsided."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: The Concept of Distributions", lecture_lines_text)
        
        # Elements for animations
        axes = Axes(x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 1], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        normal_curve = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2), color="#3498DB")
        mean_label = MathTex(r"\mu", color="#E74C3C").scale(0.8)
        sigma_label = MathTex(r"\sigma", color="#E74C3C").scale(0.8)
        
        # Load asset
        data_icon = SVGMobject("/scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/data.svg", color="#F1C40F")
        data_points = VGroup(*[data_icon.copy().scale(0.1) for _ in range(20)])
        
        area = axes.get_area(normal_curve, [-1, 1], color="#2ECC71", opacity=0.3)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.place_at_grid(VGroup(axes, normal_curve), 'B3', scale_factor=0.6)
        self.play(Create(axes), Create(normal_curve))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.place_at_grid(mean_label, 'C4', scale_factor=0.9) # Fix for issue 22
        self.place_at_grid(sigma_label, 'C5', scale_factor=0.9) # Fix for issue 23
        self.play(FadeIn(mean_label), FadeIn(sigma_label))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFFFFF"))
        self.place_at_grid(data_points, 'E3', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(FadeIn(data_points))
        self.place_in_area(area, 'B4', 'E6', scale_factor=0.8) # Fix for issue 21
        self.play(FadeIn(area))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): The Magic of Averages

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distributions
sections.content: Briefly define 'Distribution' as a shape showing how data spreads. Introduce the 'Uniform' (flat) and 'Skewed' (lopsided) distributions to establish that data doesn't always look like a bell curve.
sections.example: Visualizing a die roll: Rolling one die gives a flat distribution (equal chance for 1-6).

sections.title: The Problem: Chaos in Small Samples
sections.content: Explain that when we look at individual data points, they are unpredictable and follow the original, irregular distribution. This is the 'Chaos' phase.
sections.example: An anthropomorphic squirrel collecting nuts: One day he might find 0 nuts, the next he finds 20. His personal success is highly erratic.

sections.title: The Mechanism: The Power of Aggregation
sections.content: Introduce the CLT: As we increase the sample size (n) and take the average of those samples, the distribution of those averages begins to morph into a 'Normal Distribution' (Bell Curve), regardless of the original data shape.
sections.example: The 'Squirrel Council': Instead of tracking one squirrel, we track the average of 50 squirrels. The extreme '0 nuts' and '20 nuts' days cancel each other out, forming a predictable peak at the average.

sections.title: Visualization: The Morphing Animation
sections.content: Describe a visual transition: Start with a jagged, irregular histogram. As a counter 'n' increases from 1 to 30, show the bars shifting and smoothing out into a perfect symmetrical Bell Curve.
sections.example: An animation showing a 'chaos cloud' of dots collapsing into a neat, symmetrical mountain shape as more samples are added.

sections.title: Application: Why Does This Matter?
sections.content: Conclude with the real-world significance: The CLT allows us to make predictions about populations based on samples, forming the backbone of inferential statistics and quality control.
sections.example: Factory QC: A sensor measures the weight of thousands of candy bars. Even if the machine is slightly inconsistent, the average weight will perfectly follow a bell curve, telling the factory exactly how many bars to reject.
